paras: The Lima jail mob of 1888 was an attempt by a white crowd to lynch Black men accused of a fatal stabbing in Lima, Ohio, on the night of the city election, April 2, 1888. The mob, put at 500 to two thousand, forced its way into the county jail, beat Lew Hunter and opened every cell, but officers had hidden the accused and no one was lynched. Papers from New Hampshire to Mississippi carried the story, much of it as a wire report that overstated the deaths in the fight.

A Lima dispatch described a long "vendetta" between young Irishmen and Black men in the city, and the fullest account said the feeling ran highest on election day. According to that account, William Goins and Tim Casey fought outside a saloon about seven o'clock, and later Goins and several companions went looking for the Casey crowd.

In the fight in front of Manning Brothers' saloon on Main Street, Patrick Hughes, a sixteen-year-old, was stabbed through the heart and died, and Dave Gallagher and a man named Stockey or Stokey were badly cut. Police arrested some of the accused soon afterward and hid them, fearing mob violence.

As word spread that arrests had been made, a crowd searched the police station on High Street and then ran to the county jail, where Sheriff M. P. Hoagland refused the keys and said the men were not there. Three ringleaders were let in to inspect the cells, but the mob would not accept their report and broke in the doors. The sheriff handed the keys to Lew Hunter, whom the Maysville paper called his assistant; the mob, thinking he meant to hide them, beat him and took them, and one man tried to strike the sheriff with a piece of iron. The Macon Beacon reported that several thousand people filled the jail yard and street and that "the unanimous sentiment being that they should die," but after opening every cell the mob gave up.
The Cleveland Gazette's Lima correspondent wrote that the mob's threats made it "very dangerous for a colored man to be on the streets."

A coroner's inquest over Hughes found Frederick Harrison guilty of his murder, named Sam Thomas and Bill Stanup as the men who cut the others, and called Goins and Frank Crowder "hard-knockers." Goins and Crowder were then held at Kenton, while Thomas, Harrison and Stanup were still at large. In July the same correspondent reported that Harrison had been found guilty of manslaughter and sentenced to twenty years, and that the trial of Thomas, Goins and Crowder was put off until October. No report of an inquiry into the mob or the beating of Hunter appears in the coverage.

The first national report, a Chicago Times special printed in the Indianapolis Journal on April 3, said Hughes, Gallagher and Stockey were all "stabbed to death" by Dave Crowder and William Goins, "colored." That text ran under headlines such as "Triple Murder" and "Terrible Tragedy at Lima" in Kansas and Ohio papers on April 5, and in condensed form in a New Hampshire weekly. These items called the accused "the murderers," and a short Springfield, Ohio, brief left out the mob entirely.

The fuller dispatch framed the event in racial terms, with the Maysville paper heading it "Negroes Vs. Irish" and "A Lynching Averted" and the Macon Beacon heading it "Slashed to Death" and "Race-War." The Maysville item closed by predicting that the accused "will not last many minutes after they are found," and neither paper criticized the mob.

The Cleveland Gazette's Lima correspondent, writing among local church and social notes, called the stabbing an "atrocious crime" but spoke of men "suspected" rather than murderers. That column alone dwelt on the danger the mob posed to Black residents, and it alone followed the case through the inquest and the July sentence.

The Chicago Times wire reported three dead, while the Lima dispatch and correspondent reported only Hughes killed and Gallagher fatally or seriously wounded; no later report of a second death was found. The size of the mob was given as 500 by the Lima correspondent and "fully two thousand" by the Macon Beacon's dispatch. Early reports named Crowder and Goins as Hughes's killers, but the coroner's verdict placed the killing on Frederick Harrison. White dispatches also differed on who began the fight, the Maysville paper saying the Black men went to the saloon to "do up the Irish boys" and the Chicago Times wire describing a quarrel as two of them passed.

reader.title: Lima jail mob of 1888
bases: After a fatal election-night stabbing, a mob forced its way into the Allen County jail and searched every cell 'for lynching purposes' for the accused Black men, who had been hidden; the lynching was attempted but not carried out (A3, A9, A10).

A mob of 500 or more broke into the jail to lynch men accused of the stabbing, but the accused had been hidden and no one was killed by the mob, so this was an attempted lynching, not a lynching (A3, A9, A10).

The wire reports (A1, A2), the detailed Lima account (A9, A3) and the Cleveland Gazette's Lima correspondent (A10) independently agree that a mob forced open the jail and searched it for the accused, who were not found.

accounts.label: Chicago Times wire
accounts.gist: Three men stabbed to death by Crowder and Goins; a mob visited the police stations and jail but the accused had been arrested and hidden.

accounts.label: Detailed Lima dispatch
accounts.gist: Goins's party sought out the Casey crowd; Hughes killed and two wounded; a mob of two thousand forced its way into the jail, beat Lew Hunter, took the keys and searched every cell in vain.

accounts.label: Cleveland Gazette Lima correspondent
accounts.gist: Hughes stabbed on election evening; three men 'suspected', two captured and names withheld for fear of mob violence; a gang of 500 forced the jail open; threats endangered colored residents.

accounts.label: Coroner's verdict
accounts.gist: Frederick Harrison found guilty of Hughes's murder; Thomas and Stanup did the cutting; Goins and Crowder were 'hard-knockers'.

framing.detail: The Chicago Times wire ran as 'Two Men Killed at Lima, O.', 'Triple Murder' and 'Terrible Tragedy at Lima', calling Crowder and Goins 'the murderers' and the mob's search a response to 'intense excitement'.

Maysville headlined 'A Lima Election Riot. Negroes Vs. Irish... A Lynching Averted' and said the 'murderers will not last many minutes after they are found'; the Macon Beacon headlined 'Slashed to Death' and 'Race-War' and described the crowd's 'unanimous sentiment' that the accused should die without condemning it.
The Cleveland Gazette's Lima correspondent called the stabbing an 'atrocious crime' but wrote of 'suspected' men and stressed that the mob's 'awful threats' endangered colored residents.

record_check.record: Lew Hunter, Dave Crowder, David Crowder, William Goins, Frank Crowder
record_check.dossier: The mob's targets were the accused Black men (Goins, Crowder, and per some reports Sam Thomas and Wm. Harrison); 'Dave', 'David' and 'Frank' Crowder are variant names for one man in different reports; Lew Hunter was beaten by the mob but was not its lynching target.
The accused were 'colored'; Hunter's race is not stated.
Hunter is not called a deputy: he 'happened to be with the sheriff' or was 'Sheriff Hoagland's assistant'.

record_check.record: said to have murdered Patrick Hughes
record_check.dossier: Accused in early reports of stabbing Hughes to death; the coroner later found Frederick Harrison guilty of the murder and called Goins and Crowder 'hard-knockers'.
A white mob, 'friends of the murdered men', of 500 or 'fully two thousand'; no one named.
The mob killed no one; the one death (Hughes) came in the preceding fight. The wire's three-dead version is contradicted by fuller reports.
Supported: the mob surrounded the jail, threatened violence, broke in the doors and beat Hunter.
